newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan unions withdraw mass resignation threat.
newsitem.headline: Jordan unions withdraw mass resignation threat.

text.p: Jordan's opposition-dominated union leaders withdrew threats to resign en masse in protest over curbs on press freedoms, union sources said on Friday.
They said the decision was taken on Thursday by a council grouping 13 influential professional unions from doctors to accountants.
The unions are fierce critics of Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel and have tens of thousands of members nationwide.

"In response to mass calls from union grassroots and a wide cross-section of Jordanians to protect the unions from the unjustified onslaught against them, the union heads agreed to stay in their positions and continue their duty," said a statement by the council issued after their meeting.

Union chiefs including Laith Shubailat, a leading critic of King Hussein's close ties with Israel who heads the powerful Engineers Union, had last month given the government a month to rescind the controversial press law or face their mass resignation.

The press law, issued during a parliamentary recess just months before scheduled elections, was criticised by the U.S. group Human Rights Watch which said it appeared aimed more at barring critical reporting than protecting national interests.
Many unionists now fear implementing the threat to resign could have played into the hands of the government by allowing it to impose its own appointees and take over the popularly elected unions.
King Hussein has repeatedly attacked professional unions in recent weeks, saying their leaders were serving foreign paymasters rather than working for the good of their rank and file.

"The professional unions must clarify that these unions do not rally under any flag or group or the whim of any party or organisation or government but under the banner of the nation," the union's statement said in an indirect response to the king.
Officials have also been questioning the legality of unions, raising the spectre of a clampdown on their political activity ahead of parliamentary elections scheduled for November.
